title: General OT Security Posture
notes: High-level, interview-based OT posture assessment. Every scored question's band is set by the consultant using their judgement of the answer; the tool never derives the band from the captured fields. scored:false questions capture context only and are excluded from grading. Indicative, not a conformance or regulatory assessment.

responseModel.rule: The band is always set by the consultant. Capture fields (text, checklist, choice, boolean) inform and evidence the band but never set it.

questions.prompt: Is there a named person accountable for OT/ICS cyber security?
questions.rationale: In OT, accountability is often split between plant engineering and IT, and cyber risk to safety and availability can end up owned by neither. One named owner with real authority makes sure someone manages that risk.
questions.goodLooksLike: A named person is accountable for OT cyber security. They have a clear mandate, a say in the budget and a route to senior management, and they work alongside plant and engineering leadership.

bandAnchors.1: Informal or shared with IT, unclear
bandAnchors.2: Named owner but limited authority or time
bandAnchors.3: Named owner with a clear mandate and resources

questions.prompt: Has an OT-specific cyber risk assessment been carried out?
questions.rationale: IT risk assessments rarely capture OT consequences such as loss of view, loss of control, or harm to safety and production. Without an OT-specific assessment, controls are not prioritised against the risks that matter on the plant.
questions.goodLooksLike: A documented OT risk assessment weighs safety and availability impact and drives a prioritised improvement plan, following the approach of ISA/IEC 62443-3-2. It is refreshed periodically and after major change.

bandAnchors.1: Informal, or IT risk assessment assumed to cover OT
bandAnchors.3: Done, maintained, and used to drive decisions

questions.prompt: Are there OT security policies or standards, and do staff follow them?
questions.rationale: Policies written for IT often cannot be met in OT, for example forced patching or account lockouts, so staff ignore them and the plant is left with no working standard. OT policies that people can follow set the same expectations across shifts and contractors.
questions.goodLooksLike: OT-specific policies and standards exist and are realistic for the plant. Staff and contractors know them and follow them, and the policies are reviewed periodically.

bandAnchors.1: IT policies assumed to cover OT
bandAnchors.2: OT policies exist but adoption is patchy

questions.prompt: Does OT security feature in budgeting and management reporting?
questions.rationale: When OT security does not appear in budgets or management reports, improvements compete poorly for funding and fall away over time. Regular reporting keeps leadership aware of the residual risk they are carrying.
questions.goodLooksLike: OT cyber risk and remediation progress are reported to management regularly, and funding is allocated through the normal budget cycle.

questions.prompt: Do OT changes go through a process that considers security as well as safety and availability?
questions.rationale: OT change control is usually mature for safety and says nothing about security, so firewall rules, accounts and connections are approved on operational grounds alone. Change control is also what keeps the other controls from eroding between assessments.
questions.goodLooksLike: Management of change asks about security explicitly for OT changes. Higher-risk changes get security input, and the decision and its reasons are recorded.

bandAnchors.3: Security a defined step in change control

questions.prompt: Do OT staff and contractors get security training relevant to the plant, beyond corporate e-learning?
questions.rationale: Operators and engineers make the decisions that count, such as plugging in a USB stick, allowing a vendor connection or bypassing a control to keep the plant running. Corporate phishing training does not cover these.
questions.goodLooksLike: Operators, engineers and contractors receive OT-specific awareness training on the risks and behaviours that apply to the plant. It is refreshed periodically and reaches the shift teams.

questions.prompt: Are security expectations set with OT suppliers, and are they checked?
questions.rationale: Most work on an OT system is done by another company's engineer on another company's laptop. If the site asks nothing of its suppliers and checks nothing, it inherits the practices of its weakest supplier.
questions.goodLooksLike: Security requirements are written into OT contracts and specifications. Suppliers are asked for evidence that they meet them, and the answers count when choosing who to use.

questions.prompt: Who are the main OT security stakeholders and contacts on site?
questions.rationale: Everyday decisions depend on knowing who owns, operates and supports each part of the OT estate. In an incident the right people have to be reached quickly.
questions.goodLooksLike: The OT stakeholders and contacts in operations, engineering, safety, IT security and the vendors are identified and kept up to date. Everyone involved understands the escalation routes.

questions.prompt: Is there an inventory of OT assets?
questions.rationale: A site cannot protect, patch or monitor devices it does not know about. OT estates collect legacy and undocumented devices over time, and an incomplete inventory is one of the most common causes of OT exposure.
questions.goodLooksLike: The site keeps an inventory of its OT assets, including controllers, HMIs, network devices and their software and firmware versions. Change management keeps it current, ideally with passive discovery to check it.

questions.prompt: Is there an up-to-date network diagram for the OT environment?
questions.rationale: Segmentation, incident response and change decisions all depend on an accurate network diagram. Out-of-date drawings lead to wrong assumptions about what is connected and how.
questions.goodLooksLike: The OT network diagram shows zones, conduits, interconnections and external links. It is under version control and is updated through change management.

questions.prompt: Do staff know what is connected to the OT network, including transient and contractor devices?
questions.rationale: Transient laptops, contractor devices and forgotten connections are a common way for malware to reach OT. If staff cannot say what is connected, unauthorised or risky devices go unnoticed.
questions.goodLooksLike: The site knows what is connected to the OT network, ideally through technical monitoring, and controls the use of transient and contractor devices.

questions.prompt: Are external and vendor connections into OT documented and understood?
questions.rationale: Vendor and external links bypass perimeter controls and are one of the main ways OT systems are compromised. A connection nobody has documented cannot be risk assessed, controlled or monitored.
questions.goodLooksLike: Every external and vendor connection into OT is documented, justified, access controlled, monitored and reviewed. Links that are no longer used are removed.

questions.prompt: Is the OT network separated from the corporate / IT network?
questions.rationale: On a flat network, an IT compromise such as ransomware can spread straight into OT, stop production or threaten safety. Separating OT from IT is the most effective single control in OT.
questions.goodLooksLike: Firewalls separate OT from corporate IT, with a controlled DMZ, default-deny rules and no direct routable path between them. The separation is enforced and monitored.

bandAnchors.1: Some separation, for example VLAN only
bandAnchors.3: Firewalled boundary with a DMZ and controlled data exchange

questions.prompt: Is the OT environment divided into zones reflecting criticality, for example Purdue levels, cells, or safety?
questions.rationale: Internal zoning limits how far an intruder or malware can move and protects the most critical and safety-related functions. A single large OT zone offers no internal containment.
questions.goodLooksLike: OT is divided into zones and conduits that reflect criticality, such as Purdue levels, cells and safety systems, in line with ISA/IEC 62443-3-2. Traffic between zones passes through controlled, monitored conduits.

bandAnchors.3: Zones defined and enforced with controlled conduits

questions.prompt: How is data exchanged between IT and OT, for example historian or file transfer?
questions.rationale: Historian feeds, file transfers and similar flows are needed, but they create paths between IT and OT that attackers can use. Uncontrolled data exchange weakens segmentation without anyone noticing.
questions.goodLooksLike: Data passes between IT and OT through a DMZ, using brokered flows that are one-way where possible, for example a data diode or a replicated historian. IT has no direct access into OT.

bandAnchors.3: Via a brokered or controlled mechanism, for example DMZ historian or data diode

questions.prompt: Is remote access into OT controlled, for both vendors and staff?
questions.rationale: Remote access for vendors and staff is convenient, and it is consistently one of the most common ways into OT. Uncontrolled or always-on access exposes the plant directly.
questions.goodLooksLike: Remote access goes through a hardened gateway with MFA, least privilege, approval for each session and full logging. Vendor access is time limited and monitored.

bandAnchors.3: Brokered, per-session, and monitored, for example jump host with MFA and time limits

questions.prompt: Are safety systems (SIS) separated from the basic process control network?
questions.rationale: Safety instrumented systems are the last line of protection for people and plant. If they share a network with basic process control, one cyber event can degrade safety and control at the same time.
questions.goodLooksLike: Safety systems are separated from the basic process control network by segmentation or an air gap, consistent with IEC 61511 and ISA/IEC 62443. Any interface between them is tightly controlled and monitored.

bandAnchors.3: Separated or independent in line with accepted practice

questions.guidance: If there is no SIS on site, mark this question not applicable.

questions.prompt: Are individual user accounts used, or are shared and generic logins common?
questions.rationale: Shared and generic logins are common in OT because they are quick to use, but they remove accountability, and misuse cannot be detected or traced to a person. One compromised shared credential can expose everything it reaches.
questions.goodLooksLike: Individual accounts are used wherever the technology allows. The few shared operational accounts that remain are justified, held in a vault and monitored.

questions.prompt: Is access limited to what each role needs (least privilege)?
questions.rationale: With broad access, one compromised account can change logic, settings or safety parameters. OT roles are usually narrow, so least privilege is practical to apply and limits the damage a compromised account can do.
questions.goodLooksLike: Each role has only the access it needs, so an operator account cannot change logic or configuration. Access rights are reviewed periodically.

questions.prompt: Are default and vendor passwords changed on OT devices?
questions.rationale: Default and vendor credentials are publicly known and routinely targeted. In OT they often stay in place for years on devices that are rarely revisited.
questions.goodLooksLike: Default and vendor passwords are changed at commissioning where the device allows it, stored in a vault and checked during audits. Devices that cannot change them are covered by compensating controls.

questions.prompt: Is there a process to remove access when people leave or change role?
questions.shortTitle: Access removal on leaver or role change
questions.rationale: Leavers and movers who keep their access, especially contractors and vendors, remain an insider and supply chain risk. OT accounts are often never reviewed after they are created.
questions.goodLooksLike: A joiners, movers and leavers process removes or adjusts OT access promptly, vendor accounts included, and periodic access reviews back it up.

questions.prompt: Do OT administrators use a separate account for administrative work, apart from their everyday login?
questions.rationale: When the same account is used to read email and to administer a controller, one phishing click can give an attacker administrative control of the plant.
questions.goodLooksLike: Administrators have a separate privileged account that they use only for administrative work, never for email or web browsing. Everyday accounts hold no standing administrative rights.

questions.prompt: Can highly privileged accounts log on to ordinary OT servers and workstations?
questions.shortTitle: Where privileged accounts can log on
questions.rationale: An administrator who signs in to an engineering workstation leaves credentials there for whoever compromises it next. This is the usual way an attacker's foothold in IT becomes control of OT.
questions.goodLooksLike: Privileged accounts are tiered, so the most privileged accounts sign in only to the directory servers and to dedicated admin workstations. OT authenticates separately from corporate IT, or through a controlled one-way trust. Where a site has no central directory, shared administrative credentials are not reused across OT machines.

bandAnchors.1: Unrestricted, but recognised as a risk

capture.label: How does OT authenticate?
options: Separate OT directory, trusted by corporate

questions.prompt: How are OT systems patched or updated in practice?
questions.rationale: Uptime, vendor approval and legacy systems make OT hard to patch, so unpatched vulnerabilities build up. The aim is to patch safely, in order of risk.
questions.goodLooksLike: Patches and updates are applied through a risk-based process that follows maintenance windows and vendor guidance. Where patching is not feasible, segmentation, hardening and monitoring compensate.

bandAnchors.3: Risk-based, with compensating controls where patching is not possible

questions.prompt: Is malware protection in place where appropriate and supported?
questions.rationale: Malware, including commodity ransomware, remains one of the main causes of OT outages. Traditional antivirus can be unsafe on unsupported endpoints, so the protection has to suit OT.
questions.goodLooksLike: Supported malware protection is deployed and kept current wherever it is safe to run. Fixed-function devices use application allow-listing as well.

bandAnchors.3: Managed and OT-appropriate, including allow-listing where AV is unsuitable

questions.prompt: Is removable media, such as USB, controlled in the OT environment?
questions.rationale: USB sticks and other removable media cross air gaps and are a well-known way for infections to reach OT, including isolated systems. Uncontrolled media can bypass every other control.
questions.goodLooksLike: Removable media use is restricted, with scanning or sanitisation stations, port control or allow-listing, and a clear policy for vendors and engineers.

bandAnchors.3: Controlled, for example scanning kiosk or port control

questions.prompt: Are backups of critical OT systems taken, protected, and tested?
questions.rationale: After an OT incident, the speed of restoring controllers, HMIs and configurations decides how long the plant is down. Backups that are untested, or that ransomware can reach, fail when they are needed.
questions.goodLooksLike: Critical OT configurations and systems are backed up regularly and kept offline or immutable, apart from the OT network. Restores are tested, so the recovery time is known.

bandAnchors.3: Regular, protected (offline or immutable), and restore-tested

questions.prompt: Are OT endpoints and servers hardened, with unneeded services and ports removed?
questions.rationale: OT devices ship with services, ports and software they do not need, and each one adds to the attack surface. Hardening reduces exposure on systems that are hard to patch.
questions.goodLooksLike: OT endpoints and servers are hardened to a baseline, with unneeded services and ports removed and a secure configuration applied. Change management keeps the baseline in place.

questions.prompt: Is it known which OT systems are unsupported or end-of-life, and is that risk managed?
questions.rationale: Unsupported systems are normal in OT and often cannot be replaced on a security timescale. The usual problem is that nobody has recorded where they are, so no protection is ever put around them.
questions.goodLooksLike: End-of-life and unsupported OT systems are identified and their risk is accepted at the right level. Each one has a compensating control or a funded replacement plan.

questions.prompt: Is physical access to OT equipment controlled, including control rooms, cabinets and live network ports?
questions.rationale: Every logical control assumes that nobody can reach the hardware. An unlocked cabinet or a live port in an open area bypasses them all, and this is usually the cheapest gap on a site to close.
questions.goodLooksLike: Control rooms and equipment cabinets are secured and only people who need access have it. Unused network ports are disabled or protected, and contractors in plant areas are supervised.
references: NCSC CAF B2 (Device and physical security)

questions.prompt: Are logs collected from OT systems?
questions.rationale: Without logs from OT systems, an incident cannot be investigated and nobody can show what happened. Many OT devices have logging turned off, or keep no logs, by default.
questions.goodLooksLike: Relevant logs are collected centrally, time-synchronised and retained. Sources include HMIs, jump hosts, OT network devices, security tools and, where possible, controllers.

questions.prompt: Is there monitoring that would detect an intrusion or abnormal activity in OT?
questions.rationale: OT intrusions can go unnoticed for months. Passive OT monitoring detects abnormal activity and new devices without disturbing the process.
questions.goodLooksLike: OT monitoring, such as passive network detection, is in place and tuned to the environment. Someone with OT knowledge triages the alerts.

questions.prompt: If something happened tonight, would anyone notice, and who?
questions.rationale: Detection is only useful if someone can see the alert and act on it out of hours. Many sites have the tools and nobody watching them, so events go unanswered.
questions.goodLooksLike: Alerts reach a defined team, such as a SOC or an on-call rota, at any hour, and that team has OT escalation routes.

bandAnchors.3: Yes, with defined alerting and on-call

questions.prompt: Does anyone review OT security events, or are the logs opened only after something goes wrong?
questions.rationale: Logs that are collected and never reviewed do not detect anything. Many sites hold OT logs that nobody looks at until an investigation needs them.
questions.goodLooksLike: OT events are reviewed on a set schedule and a named team triages alerts. Staff have an easy way to report anything that looks wrong.
references: NCSC CAF C2 (Proactive security event discovery)

bandAnchors.3: Triaged routinely, with a reporting route

questions.prompt: If something were discovered a month later, would enough be recorded to reconstruct it?
questions.rationale: OT intrusions are usually found long after they begin. Retention decides whether an investigation can show what happened or can only confirm that something did.
questions.goodLooksLike: OT records are kept long enough to investigate an incident found late, are protected from tampering and cover the systems that matter.

questions.prompt: Is there an incident response plan that explicitly covers OT?
questions.rationale: Generic IT incident plans call for actions such as isolating, wiping or rebooting systems, which can be unsafe in OT. An OT-specific plan protects safety and production during the response.
questions.goodLooksLike: The incident response plan covers OT scenarios, roles, safe containment actions and who has authority to decide. It can be reached during an outage.

bandAnchors.3: OT-specific plan with roles and contacts

questions.prompt: Do plant or engineering and security know how to work together in an incident?
questions.rationale: OT incidents need plant or engineering staff and security staff to act together. If they have never agreed how, the response is slow and decisions conflict, which puts safety and uptime at risk.
questions.goodLooksLike: Plant or engineering and security have agreed and rehearsed how they work together in an incident, with clear roles and a shared communication route.

questions.prompt: Can critical OT systems be recovered to a known good state, and how quickly?
questions.shortTitle: Recovery to a known good state
questions.rationale: How quickly critical systems can be returned to a known good state largely sets how long an OT outage lasts. Slow or uncertain recovery also adds pressure to take unsafe shortcuts.
questions.goodLooksLike: Critical OT systems can be restored to a known good state from protected backups within a known and acceptable time, and the site has shown this in a test.

bandAnchors.3: Documented and tested recovery within a known time

questions.prompt: Have any exercises or tabletops been run for an OT incident?
questions.rationale: Plans that are never exercised tend to fail under pressure. A tabletop exercise exposes gaps in roles, contacts and safe actions before a real OT incident does.
questions.goodLooksLike: OT incident scenarios are exercised periodically, as tabletop or live exercises, with operations and engineering taking part. Lessons learned are fed back into the plan.

questions.prompt: Could the plant keep running, or come down safely, with the control system unavailable?
questions.rationale: A site that can fall back to manual operation or a safe shutdown while the control system is rebuilt has hours or days to recover properly. A site that cannot is forced into hurried decisions.
questions.goodLooksLike: Degraded and manual modes of operation are identified and documented, and operators have practised them. The fallback does not depend on the systems that would be unavailable.
references: NCSC CAF D1 (Response and recovery planning)
